attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, endorsed. The surrounding quotes from the email and The New Yorker are not part of the claim.

semantics.note: Mostly faithful. The normalised text drops 'decisively', but the contract keeps it as an explicit element. This is a retrospective interpretive observation about OpenAI's intent from 2016 onward.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair. Because Marcus said 'shows decisively', a high bar is justified. Telling a conditional expectation of future reduced openness apart from a settled intent that contradicts public statements is an interpretation Marcus did not supply, and it decides the result.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own publication of the January 2016 Sutskever email: 'it will make sense to start being less open'. This supports an early intent of reduced openness. It is a company disclosure and is conditional on getting closer to AI.
The December 2015 founding announcement encourages publication and free collaboration but does not promise to release everything. It sets the public baseline for comparison.

Ars Technica reproduces the full qualification: sharing everything is right in the short and possibly medium term, for recruitment. This shows openness was partly instrumental, but it was also actually intended near-term, which complicates the claim of 'no intention'.

reviews.rationale: The part that holds: the January 2016 email shows that early leadership expected to become less open than the name suggested, and saw near-term sharing partly as a recruitment tool. The part not established: that it 'decisively' proves a settled intent contrary to public statements. The founding announcement was qualified (encouraged to publish), and the email is conditional on future progress and endorses full sharing in the near term.
